listening.title: See tiny organisms on show in microscopic video competition
listening.topic: Nikon's Small World In Motion competition showcases stunning microscopic videos of tiny organisms filmed through microscopes.
listening.topic_zh: 尼康「小世界動態」競賽展示透過顯微鏡拍攝的微小生物精彩影片。
listening.transcript_excerpt: Every year, scientists and filmmakers from around the world submit extraordinary footage to Nikon's Small World In Motion competition, a prestigious event that celebrates the art and science of microscopic videography. This year's winning entry was particularly remarkable — a video magnified one hundred times, revealing the intricate movements of cilia, which are tiny hair-like structures found in the airways of a child suffering from a rare genetic disease. The footage was captured by Dr Ning Xu, a dedicated researcher at Tsinghua University in China, who employed a sophisticated technique involving complex light waves to illuminate different sections of the biological sample in vivid colour. The result was a breathtaking visual journey into a world invisible to the naked eye. Other impressive entries included a video of a roundworm coming into contact with a single-celled organism, as well as microscopic jellyfish larvae delicately suspended within droplets of water. Among the highly commended clips were images of bioluminescent algae glowing in the dark and a tiny sea slug navigating its miniature environment. These videos remind us that an entire universe of biological complexity exists just beyond the limits of human vision, and that advances in microscopy are opening new windows into life at its smallest and most fundamental scale.

vocabulary.definition: Microscopic hair-like structures on the surface of cells that move rhythmically to transport fluids or particles across cell surfaces.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 纖毛：細胞表面微小的毛髮狀結構，能有節奏地擺動以輸送液體或顆粒。
vocabulary.example: The cilia lining the respiratory tract help to sweep mucus and debris away from the lungs.

vocabulary.definition: Made to appear larger than actual size, typically through the use of a lens or microscope.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 放大的：透過鏡頭或顯微鏡使物體看起來比實際尺寸更大。
vocabulary.example: The magnified image revealed intricate cellular structures that would otherwise be impossible to observe.

vocabulary.definition: Describing living organisms that produce and emit light through chemical reactions within their bodies.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 生物發光的：描述能透過體內化學反應產生並發出光的生物。
vocabulary.example: Bioluminescent algae create a stunning blue glow on the surface of the ocean at night.

vocabulary.definition: To light up or make something visible by shining light upon it; also used figuratively to mean making something clearer or easier to understand.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 照亮：用光照射使某物可見；也可比喻使某事更清晰或易於理解。
vocabulary.example: The researcher used specialised light waves to illuminate different layers of the tissue sample.

vocabulary.definition: A filming technique in which frames are captured at a much slower rate than normal, so that when played back at standard speed, events appear to happen much faster.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 縮時攝影：一種拍攝技術，以比正常慢得多的速度捕捉畫面，回放時事件看起來發生得更快。
vocabulary.example: Time-lapse photography was used to capture the gradual blooming of a flower over several days.

options: A: Bioluminescent algae glowing in ocean water

options: A: Standard white-light microscopy with digital filters
B: Time-lapse photography combined with ultraviolet radiation
C: Complex light waves to illuminate different parts of the sample in colour
D: Bioluminescent chemical reactions within the tissue itself

options: A: Microscopic jellyfish larvae suspended in droplets of water
B: A roundworm encountering a single-celled organism
C: Bioluminescent algae and a tiny sea slug

reading.title: Microscopic Videography: Revealing the Hidden World of Tiny Organisms
reading.passage:
The natural world conceals an entire dimension of biological activity that lies beyond the reach of the unaided human eye. Microscopic videography — the practice of filming living organisms and biological processes through a microscope — has emerged as a powerful tool for both scientific research and public education, bridging the gap between laboratory discovery and wider human understanding.

Nikon's annual Small World In Motion competition represents one of the most prominent platforms for this discipline. Open to participants from across the globe, the competition invites scientists, researchers, and photography enthusiasts to submit video footage captured through microscopes, celebrating both technical innovation and artistic vision. Entries are evaluated on the basis of their scientific significance, visual quality, and the complexity of the techniques employed.

This year's winning submission, produced by Dr Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China, depicted cilia — microscopic, hair-like projections found on the surface of epithelial cells — beating rhythmically within the airways of a child diagnosed with a rare genetic disorder. The footage, magnified one hundred times, was made possible by an advanced illumination method in which multiple wavelengths of light were directed at different regions of the biological sample, rendering distinct cellular components in vivid colour. This technique enabled viewers to observe the precise mechanical dysfunction associated with the child's condition, offering potential insights for medical research.

Among the runners up were videos documenting a roundworm's encounter with a single-celled organism and microscopic jellyfish larvae suspended within water droplets. Highly commended entries featured bioluminescent algae — organisms capable of generating their own light through biochemical processes — as well as a diminutive sea slug navigating its aquatic habitat.

The competition underscores the growing intersection between scientific inquiry and visual storytelling. As microscopy technology continues to advance, such competitions are likely to yield increasingly detailed and diagnostically valuable imagery, transforming public perception of the microscopic world and accelerating biological discovery.

questions.statement: The Nikon Small World In Motion competition is restricted to professional scientists and academic researchers.
questions.explanation: The passage states the competition is open to participants from across the globe, including scientists, researchers, and photography enthusiasts, indicating it is not restricted to professionals.

questions.statement: Dr Ning Xu's winning video used different wavelengths of light to distinguish between cellular components in colour.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that Dr Ning Xu directed multiple wavelengths of light at different regions of the sample, rendering distinct cellular components in vivid colour.

questions.statement: The judges of the competition ranked bioluminescent algae footage above the roundworm video in the final results.
questions.explanation: The passage mentions that bioluminescent algae were highly commended and the roundworm video was a runner up, but no explicit ranking comparison between these two entries is provided.

questions.q: According to the passage, what is one potential benefit of Dr Ning Xu's winning footage?
options: A: It provides a definitive cure for the child's rare genetic disorder
B: It demonstrates that time-lapse photography is superior to standard microscopy
C: It may offer insights relevant to medical research into cellular dysfunction
D: It proves that cilia are absent in healthy human airways
questions.explanation: The passage states that the footage offered potential insights for medical research by enabling viewers to observe the precise mechanical dysfunction associated with the child's condition, making option C the most accurate answer.

speaking.topic: Describe a scientific discovery or technological advancement that you found particularly fascinating.
speaking.topic_zh: 描述一項你覺得特別令人著迷的科學發現或技術進步。

part2.cue_card:
Describe a scientific discovery or technological advancement that you found particularly fascinating.

You should say:
• What the discovery or advancement is
• How you first learned about it
• Why you found it so interesting or impressive

And explain how you think it could affect people's lives in the future.

You will have one minute to prepare. You should speak for one to two minutes.
band_tips: Use sophisticated scientific vocabulary naturally and accurately, such as 'microscopic', 'illuminate', 'bioluminescent', and 'magnification', to demonstrate lexical range without sounding forced.

Develop your answer by moving beyond simple description — discuss the emotional impact it had on you, the broader scientific implications, and speculate about future developments using a range of conditional structures such as 'should this technology advance further' or 'were such tools more widely available'.

Demonstrate grammatical range by mixing complex sentence structures, including relative clauses, passive constructions, and hypothetical conditionals, to achieve the fluency and accuracy expected at Band 7 and above.

part3.q: Why do you think scientific competitions like the Nikon Small World In Motion contest are important for society?
part3.q_zh: 你認為像尼康「小世界動態」這樣的科學競賽對社會為何重要？
key_points: Such competitions democratise science by making complex research accessible and visually engaging to the general public, breaking down barriers between specialists and laypeople.
They incentivise innovation by rewarding creative and technically sophisticated approaches to scientific documentation, potentially accelerating progress in fields such as medicine and biology.
They foster a culture of scientific curiosity, particularly among younger generations who may be inspired to pursue careers in research or technology after engaging with compelling visual content.

part3.q: Do you think technology has made it easier or harder for ordinary people to appreciate and understand science? Why?
part3.q_zh: 你認為科技讓普通人更容易還是更難欣賞和理解科學？為什麼？
key_points: Digital platforms and high-quality visual media have made scientific concepts far more accessible, allowing complex phenomena such as microscopic biology to be communicated through striking imagery rather than dense academic text.

However, the overwhelming volume of online information can create confusion, particularly when misinformation spreads as rapidly as verified scientific findings, making critical evaluation more challenging for non-specialists.

Interactive tools, documentaries, and citizen science projects represent promising middle ground, actively engaging the public in scientific processes rather than positioning them as passive consumers of information.

part3.q: Some people argue that governments should invest more in scientific research that has no immediate practical application. Do you agree?
part3.q_zh: 有些人認為政府應該在沒有立即實際應用的科學研究上投入更多資金。你同意嗎？
key_points: Fundamental or 'blue sky' research has historically produced transformative breakthroughs — the internet and many life-saving medical treatments originated from research with no foreseeable practical application at the time of discovery.

From a purely economic perspective, governments face pressure to prioritise research that delivers measurable returns on investment, which may lead to underfunding of theoretical disciplines such as particle physics or pure mathematics.

A balanced funding model that supports both applied and fundamental research is arguably the most prudent approach, recognising that today's seemingly abstract discovery may become tomorrow's indispensable technology.

part3.q: How might advances in microscopy and biological imaging change the future of medicine?
part3.q_zh: 顯微鏡和生物成像技術的進步可能如何改變未來的醫學？
key_points: Enhanced imaging technologies could enable earlier and more precise diagnosis of diseases at a cellular level, potentially identifying conditions such as cancer or genetic disorders before conventional symptoms become apparent.

Real-time microscopic visualisation of biological processes could revolutionise surgical procedures, allowing surgeons to operate with unprecedented precision and minimise damage to surrounding healthy tissue.

A deeper understanding of cellular mechanics — such as the dysfunction of cilia observed in the Nikon competition's winning video — could lead to the development of targeted therapies that address the root causes of genetic diseases rather than merely managing their symptoms.

writing.task2_question: Scientific competitions and awards play an increasingly important role in encouraging research and innovation. Some people believe that such competitions are the most effective way to drive scientific progress, while others argue that consistent government funding and institutional support are more valuable. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
writing.task2_question_zh: 科學競賽和獎項在鼓勵研究與創新方面扮演越來越重要的角色。有些人認為此類競賽是推動科學進步最有效的方式，而另一些人則認為持續的政府資助和機構支持更有價值。討論兩種觀點並給出你自己的意見。

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use in the introduction or body paragraphs to present a broadly accepted fact or perspective before developing your argument.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於引言或段落開頭，呈現一個被廣泛接受的事實或觀點，然後再發展你的論點。
useful_phrases.example: It is widely acknowledged that scientific competitions have the power to inspire public interest in research fields that might otherwise seem inaccessible.

useful_phrases.phrase: proponents of this view argue that
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when presenting the perspective you are about to discuss, particularly when outlining the position you may or may not personally support.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於介紹你即將討論的觀點，特別是在概述你可能支持或不支持的立場時。
useful_phrases.example: Proponents of this view argue that without sustained institutional funding, even the most promising scientific breakthroughs risk being abandoned before they reach their full potential.

useful_phrases.phrase: while this perspective has considerable merit
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use as a transition between two contrasting viewpoints to acknowledge the validity of one argument before presenting a counterargument or your own position.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於兩個對比觀點之間的過渡，在提出反駁或個人立場前承認某一論點的合理性。
useful_phrases.example: While this perspective has considerable merit, it overlooks the extent to which competitive incentives can galvanise researchers who might otherwise lack the motivation to pursue novel approaches.

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when drawing a conclusion from examples or reasoning presented earlier in your paragraph, to give your argument an evidence-based, academic tone.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 在段落中根據之前提出的例子或推理得出結論時使用，使論點具有以證據為基礎的學術語氣。
useful_phrases.example: The evidence suggests that a synergistic relationship between competitive awards and government funding produces the most significant and sustained advances in scientific knowledge.

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use in the conclusion to signal that you are delivering your ultimate judgement after weighing the arguments presented throughout the essay.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於結論段，表示你在權衡全文論點後給出最終判斷。
useful_phrases.example: In the final analysis, neither competitions nor institutional funding alone can fully sustain the breadth and depth of scientific progress that modern society demands.

outline.intro: Begin by contextualising the growing importance of scientific innovation in the modern world, briefly define both positions — the value of competitions versus sustained institutional funding — and conclude the introduction with a clear thesis stating that both mechanisms play complementary roles, though consistent funding forms the more reliable foundation.
outline.body1: Present the argument in favour of scientific competitions: they generate public enthusiasm, incentivise creative approaches, attract interdisciplinary talent, and can rapidly elevate lesser-known research to global prominence, as demonstrated by events such as Nikon's Small World In Motion competition. Acknowledge that the prestige and visibility offered by such competitions can attract further investment and institutional support.
outline.body2: Present the argument for consistent government and institutional funding: competitions are inherently selective and unpredictable, benefiting only a small number of researchers, whereas stable funding enables long-term, methodical research that may not produce visually spectacular results but yields foundational scientific knowledge. Introduce your own opinion here — that while competitions add value, they cannot substitute for the structural support that sustained funding provides.
outline.conclusion: Restate your position concisely without introducing new arguments: effective scientific progress requires both the motivational spark of competition and the structural reliability of institutional investment. Suggest that policymakers design frameworks in which competitive awards complement rather than replace sustained funding commitments, ensuring that innovation is both incentivised and adequately resourced.
